name: Formestane (Lentaron)
lead: Formestane, sold as Lentaron, is a steroidal aromatase inhibitor that was given as an intramuscular depot injection to treat estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It is not orally active, was not approved by the US FDA, and the injectable form used in Europe has been withdrawn.[1]

In looks-focused muscle-building communities the interest is in estrogen control. Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, and people who use anabolic steroids or prohormones sometimes want to limit estrogen-related effects such as water retention and breast-tissue sensitivity so that a leaner, drier physique is easier to hold. Wikipedia notes that formestane has been used to suppress estrogen arising from anabolic steroids or prohormones.[1] On T Nation, users have listed it alongside other aromatase inhibitors as something to have on hand, and some describe topical or injected formestane products they used themselves.[11][12]

Published research on formestane is almost entirely from breast cancer trials in the 1990s and early 2000s, including phase II and phase III studies against tamoxifen and megestrol acetate.[7][8][9] No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes in healthy people.
infobox: Steroidal aromatase inhibitor (second generation, Type I)

paras: The labelled use was postmenopausal estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer.[1] Aromatase inhibitors as a class are used in breast cancer because local estrogen synthesis in breast tissue fuels many tumours.[2]

Outside oncology, Wikipedia records use to suppress estrogen produced from anabolic steroids and prohormones.[1] Forum posts on T Nation mention formestane among aromatase inhibitors (Arimidex, Aromasin, letrozole) that members keep on hand during or after androgen use, and one describes using a topical formulation and then injecting it.[11][12][13] Doping-control literature also lists formestane as a prohibited anti-estrogenic substance and has characterised its urinary metabolites for testing.[10][14]

A 1994 phase III multicentre randomised comparison of formestane with tamoxifen as first-line hormonal therapy in postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer is in the literature.[6] A Swiss phase III randomised crossover trial (SAKK 20/90) compared formestane with megestrol acetate as second-line therapy after tamoxifen failure.[15] A review of phase III experience reported that Lentaron's efficacy matched tamoxifen and megestrol acetate, with 54 and 51 percent of patients in two phase III trials achieving an objective response or stable disease.[5]

Phase II work included a study of 72 postmenopausal patients given 250 mg intramuscularly every two weeks to measure serum estradiol and clinical activity,[8] a randomised comparison of two doses,[9] and a 34-patient Chinese trial of Lentaron at the same dose in recurrent or metastatic disease.[7] A 2006 meta-analysis of aromatase inhibitors and inactivators versus standard hormonal therapy in advanced breast cancer examined survival across the drug class.[3] A 1999 French review noted that formestane's response rates were not different from aminoglutethimide's and that its clinical development stopped as more potent, more specific agents (letrozole, vorozole, exemestane, anastrozole) arrived.[16]

Formestane is a structural analogue of androstenedione and a Type I steroidal, irreversible inhibitor that binds the substrate site of aromatase. It acts as a prohormone to 4-hydroxytestosterone, a weak androgen and weak aromatase inhibitor.[1] An intramuscular regimen is reported to produce roughly 85 to 92.5 percent aromatase inhibition in postmenopausal women, and it is placed in the second generation of aromatase inhibitors, ahead of third-generation drugs such as anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane.[1][17]

Reviews describe two classes of inhibitor: steroidal agents that bind competitively and irreversibly, such as formestane and exemestane, and non-steroidal agents that interfere with the enzyme's heme group, such as anastrozole and letrozole.[17][18] A 2007 review of letrozole's discovery states that letrozole is more potent than formestane and suppresses estrogen more completely.[19] Pharmacokinetic and metabolism studies in breast cancer patients, and a later study of its metabolites in humans for antidoping analysis, have been published.[10][14]
Formestane is 4-hydroxyandrost-4-ene-3,17-dione (C19H26O3), made from androstenedione via a 4,5-epoxy intermediate.[1]

Clinical studies concern breast cancer. The principal designs were phase II dose and activity studies, phase III randomised comparisons against tamoxifen and megestrol acetate, and a small Chinese single-arm trial.[5][6][7][8][9][15] The history of aromatase inhibitor development describes steroidal agents such as formestane as early successors to first-generation drugs like aminoglutethimide.[4] No studies were found testing formestane for appearance, muscle or estrogen control in healthy users.

Aromatase was identified as the enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, and investigators recognised early that blocking it could treat hormone-dependent breast cancer.[4] Formestane's synthesis from androstenedione is described in patents dating from 1959 to 1988, and Wikipedia cites a 1980 US patent naming Brodie and colleagues.[1] Lentaron was the first commercially available aromatase inhibitor in the clinic, given as a depot injection.[5] Third-generation inhibitors later replaced it in routine practice.[16][19]

Formestane was never FDA-approved and the European injectable has been withdrawn.[1] The T Nation threads that mention it are from 2004 to 2020 and place it with other estrogen-control agents in discussions of cycles and post-cycle recovery.[11][13][20] Posts also describe contest rules that list formestane (4-hydroxytestosterone) among banned hormonal precursors.[21]

timeline.event: A patent assigned to G.D. Searle is among those cited for formestane's chemistry.[1]
A US patent by Brodie and colleagues is cited for formestane.[1]
Phase II and phase III formestane trials in advanced breast cancer, including a comparison with tamoxifen, are published.[6][8][9]
The Swiss SAKK 20/90 trial against megestrol acetate is published.[15]
A study identifies urinary metabolites of formestane for antidoping analysis.[14]

lore.intro: Formestane appears on T Nation mainly as one name in lists of aromatase inhibitors used around androgen cycles.[12][13]

claims.claim: Formestane controls estrogen side effects during steroid use.
claims.believers: Posters name it among the aromatase inhibitors (with Arimidex, Aromasin and letrozole) to keep on hand against gyno and estrogen symptoms.[13][20]
claims.experts: Trials of formestane were in breast cancer, where it lowered estrogen in postmenopausal women; no study has tested it in healthy people using anabolic steroids.[7][8]

claims.claim: A topical form of formestane is an over-the-counter aromatase inhibitor.
claims.believers: One poster said he used topical formestane because his doctor would not prescribe an AI.[11]
claims.experts: The clinical formulation was an intramuscular depot and the drug is not orally active; the Wikipedia article says it was never FDA-approved.[1]

claims.claim: Formestane can be used for recovery after a cycle.
claims.believers: A poster asked whether formestane or Arimistane could serve as post-cycle support.[22]
claims.experts: No published study has examined formestane for that use.

card.summary: An injectable steroidal aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer, now withdrawn; nothing tested for looks.

quick.overview:
Formestane (Lentaron) is an injectable steroidal aromatase inhibitor used for postmenopausal breast cancer. It is not orally active and the European product has been withdrawn.
It is mentioned in bodybuilding contexts as an estrogen suppressant, but no appearance trials exist.
quick.mechanism: It irreversibly binds aromatase and blocks estrogen synthesis; it also converts to 4-hydroxytestosterone, a weak androgen.
quick.risks: It was not FDA-approved and the injectable has been withdrawn in Europe.

chain: Blocks aromatase and lowers estrogen synthesis
Reduces estrogen-linked effects in people using aromatizing androgens
Leaner, drier-looking physique and less breast-tissue sensitivity, as users describe it
angle.text: Bodybuilding users describe formestane as a way to control estrogen while using aromatizing androgens, aiming for a drier look with less water retention and chest tenderness. These are user-reported aims; the clinical research concerns breast cancer.
